decks.w2: Week 2 · Preparing for the global entrepreneurial journey

flashcards.front: The two course intended learning outcomes (CILOs) of International New Venture
flashcards.back: CILO 1: identify international market opportunities and the international business environment (Weeks 1–5). CILO 2: analyze a business model and strategic plan suitable for international expansion (Weeks 6–7).

flashcards.front: The seven weekly topics in order
flashcards.back: (1) Understanding international entrepreneurship; (2) preparing for the global entrepreneurial journey; (3) global opportunity recognition and ideation; (4) industry and market analysis; (5) business models for international markets; (6) prototyping and validation across cultures; (7) legal consideration and asset protection abroad.

flashcards.front: The three cases and the week each sits beside
flashcards.back: EuroDisneyland (Week 1, a proven model failing abroad); LocalBite (Week 2, a student founder held back by myths); FreshMart (Week 5, separating business model from value proposition and choosing a model change).

flashcards.front: The format of case work shown by the FreshMart case
flashcards.back: A short case followed by three questions worth 30, 40 and 30 points: the business model, value creation and capture, and business model development with a risk and a test.

flashcards.front: Main textbook behind the slide decks
flashcards.back: Launching New Ventures (Chapters 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7), supported by Entrepreneurship: Theory, Process, Practice.

flashcards.front: Why the order of the weeks matters
flashcards.back: Each week supplies what the next needs: a framed problem (Week 3) before industry and market tests (Week 4), those before the business model (Week 5), a validated product (Week 6) before protecting it (Week 7).

flashcards.front: Stevenson's definition of entrepreneurship
flashcards.back: "The process by which individuals, either on their own or inside organizations, pursue opportunities without regard to the resources they currently control."

flashcards.front: The four traits of the entrepreneurial way of thinking
flashcards.back: Opportunity-focused, risk-taking, innovative and growth-oriented.

flashcards.front: Phase 1 of the entrepreneurial process
flashcards.back: Find a significant problem or need; do preliminary research on the industry, market and any intellectual property, regulatory or product development issues; develop hypotheses.

flashcards.front: Phase 2 of the entrepreneurial process
flashcards.back: Validate the hypotheses about the customer, the solution and the business model; the results show potential revenue sources and major cost drivers.

flashcards.front: Phase 3 of the entrepreneurial process
flashcards.back: Once Phases 1 and 2 give sufficient confidence, design the business and plan execution: the right team and partners, and the best time to launch.

flashcards.front: The five environmental variables a new venture keeps responding to
flashcards.back: The economic environment, competition, new laws and regulations, labor supply, and sources of capital.

flashcards.front: Why the entrepreneurial process is called a dynamic system
flashcards.back: It is not linear: phases loop back when hypotheses fail, and testing continues after launch because the environment keeps changing.

flashcards.front: Four signals that lead to technological change
flashcards.back: New customer segments emerging; new customer needs; existing needs not satisfied; new ways of manufacturing and distributing products and services.

flashcards.front: How new industries are born
flashcards.back: When technological change produces a novel opportunity that enterprising entrepreneurs seize.

flashcards.front: The Week 1 description of the industry life cycle
flashcards.back: Industries are born, grow, decline and die, like humans.

flashcards.front: The three Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) economy types
flashcards.back: Factor-driven (unskilled labor, natural resources, necessity entrepreneurship), efficiency-driven (improving production and quality), innovation-driven (compete on innovation and entrepreneurship).

flashcards.front: Why factor-driven economies show very high entrepreneurial activity
flashcards.back: Businesses are often created out of necessity.

flashcards.front: The age group with the most intention to start a business (GEM)
flashcards.back: People aged 25 to 34, across all types of economies.

flashcards.front: Three characteristics of high-impact ventures
flashcards.back: Innovative (something new), value-creating (new jobs not drawn from existing firms; unserved needs), growth-oriented (regional, national or global ambition).

flashcards.front: The fuzzy front end
flashcards.back: The period before launch and startup, when activities are unclear and change as more information is obtained; much new venture risk sits here.

flashcards.front: Three things nascent entrepreneurs estimate in the fuzzy front end
flashcards.back: The probability of success; what success means as a return on time, money and effort; the risk or cost of failure.

flashcards.front: How entrepreneurs reduce subjective risk estimates
flashcards.back: Gather sufficient information and test the business model.

flashcards.front: Four reasons new businesses fail
flashcards.back: A solution looking for a problem; a "me-too" solution that is not unique; value proposition not communicated effectively; no tested business model that works.

flashcards.front: When "entrepreneur" came into popular use in the United States
flashcards.back: The 1980s, called the decade of entrepreneurship.

flashcards.front: The four trends of the 2016 textbook edition
flashcards.back: Digital anonymity, domestic manufacturing, big data and the lean startup movement.

flashcards.front: Three technology trend headings for 2018 and beyond
flashcards.back: Intelligent technology (artificial intelligence), the digital environment (immersive experiences, digital twins), and disruption (synthetic biology and genomics, quantum computing).

flashcards.front: A digital twin
flashcards.back: A digital replica of a human or real-world entity, fed by connected sensors, allowing advanced simulation, operation and analysis.

flashcards.front: EuroDisneyland's first-year headline numbers
flashcards.back: Net loss of FFr188 million for fiscal 1992; about $500 million cumulative losses by April 1993; about 10 million visitors against an 11 million target; French only 29% of visitors (forecast 50%); hotel occupancy 37%.

flashcards.front: Why EuroDisney lost money despite beating its stated break-even
flashcards.back: The 7–8 million visitor break-even was set for the $1 billion plan; construction cost estimates rose to $4.4 billion and the break-even was never updated.

flashcards.front: Spend-to-admission ratio: EuroDisney versus Tokyo
flashcards.back: EuroDisney $37.50 ÷ $47 ≈ 0.80×; Tokyo $77.50 ÷ $38 ≈ 2.04×. EuroDisney charged the highest ticket but collected the lowest total spend.

flashcards.front: How Disney's deal differed in Tokyo and Paris
flashcards.back: Tokyo: no equity, a license paying 10% of admissions, 5% of food and merchandise, plus fees. Paris: 49% equity for $160 million, management control, the same royalties plus management fees and 49% of profits.

flashcards.front: Why Disney earned while EuroDisney shareholders lost
flashcards.back: Royalties (10% admissions, 5% food, merchandise and hotels) and base management fees were charged on revenue, not profit.

flashcards.front: Three cultural misfits in EuroDisneyland
flashcards.back: No alcohol in a wine-drinking country; mainly American food; a strict United States appearance code challenged under French labor law. Intellectuals called it a "cultural Chernobyl."

flashcards.front: The recommended turnaround sequence (Option E)
flashcards.back: Fix the financial model first (capital, debt rescheduling, freeze Phase Two), then fix the product (prices, wine and beer, menus), then reinvest in a major new attraction.

flashcards.front: Why Tokyo Disneyland succeeded as a copy of Anaheim
flashcards.back: Japanese visitors wanted the "real thing" American experience; 30 million people lived within 30 miles; omiage gift-giving drove spending (over $1 billion in 1988).

flashcards.front: Five lessons from EuroDisneyland for international ventures
flashcards.back: Product-market fit first; past success does not travel automatically; recalculate break-even on the latest cost; set price to the segment; heavy debt plus high operating cost is risky.

flashcards.front: What research says about the "entrepreneur type"
flashcards.back: No psychological or sociological characteristics predict with any certainty who will become an entrepreneur or who will succeed.

flashcards.front: The six myths of entrepreneurship
flashcards.back: (1) It takes a lot of money; (2) it takes a great idea; (3) the bigger the risk, the bigger the reward; (4) a business plan is required for success; (5) entrepreneurship is for the young and reckless; (6) entrepreneurship cannot be taught.

flashcards.front: Reality behind Myth 2 (it takes a great idea)
flashcards.back: Most businesses successful for 50+ years started with a great team wanting an enduring company; usually the execution plan, not the idea, makes the business a success.

flashcards.front: Reality behind Myth 3 (bigger risk, bigger reward)
flashcards.back: Risk is relative; entrepreneurs and investors aim to reduce it. Investors expect founders to test the market, acquire the first customer and invest their own capital.

flashcards.front: Current thinking that replaces Myth 4 (business plan required)
flashcards.back: (1) Get in front of customers to test the idea, and (2) have a plan in order to grow the business.

flashcards.front: Drucker's quotation against Myth 6
flashcards.back: "It's not magic, it's not mysterious, and it has nothing to do with the genes. It is a discipline. And, like any discipline, it can be learned."

flashcards.front: Reality behind Myth 5 (young and reckless)
flashcards.back: Entrepreneurs' ages are fairly evenly distributed across all decades; entrepreneurship can be a lifetime endeavor.

flashcards.front: Two basic motives for starting a business
flashcards.back: Necessity or opportunity.

flashcards.front: Four conditions under which people choose the startup process
flashcards.back: Low industry entry barriers; uncertainty in the job market; plentiful investment capital; a breakthrough or disruptive technology that will make previous technology obsolete.

flashcards.front: Serial versus portfolio entrepreneur
flashcards.back: Serial: starts one business, then moves on to start another. Portfolio: owns minority or majority stakes in several ventures at once.

flashcards.front: The profit rule for nonprofit ventures
flashcards.back: They can and should make a profit, but the profit must stay within the organization rather than go to owners.

flashcards.front: The four corporate entrepreneurship models in order
flashcards.back: Opportunistic (waits for champions), enabler (spreads resources with clear selection criteria), advocate (assigns ownership plus modest seed funding), producer (formal unit, dedicated funds, autonomy; once called a skunkworks).

flashcards.front: Three things corporate entrepreneurs need to do
flashcards.back: Align with key decision makers; work with only the best, most motivated people; do any job needed to make the project work.

flashcards.front: Share of small businesses that were home-based (Small Business Administration, 2014)
flashcards.back: 52 percent.

flashcards.front: Five challenges of the entrepreneurial career (any five)
flashcards.back: Finding the right opportunity; long unpaid hours; uncertainty and high risk; decisions affecting others; relying on others; no previous experience; facing failure; finding the right people; raising capital; isolation and disillusionment.

flashcards.front: The six steps to prepare for entrepreneurship
flashcards.back: Find a mentor; build a professional network; learn about entrepreneurs; understand personality and business preferences; improve or acquire critical skills; study an industry.

flashcards.front: Three reasons startups expose founders to more risk
flashcards.back: They are typically undercapitalized, poorly managed and undifferentiated from competitors.

flashcards.front: Definition of networking
flashcards.back: The exchange of information and resources among individuals, groups or organizations whose common goals are to mutually benefit and create value for the members.

flashcards.front: Strong ties versus weak ties
flashcards.back: Strong ties: close friends and family. Weak ties: acquaintances and business contacts, who are not biased by prior history and so give objective advice that helps entrepreneurs move faster.

flashcards.front: Network brokers
flashcards.back: Opinion leaders who exert influence between groups and serve as gateways to other networks.

flashcards.front: Six barriers to becoming self-employed
flashcards.back: Lack of confidence; financial needs; startup logistics; personal or family issues; time constraints; lack of skills.

flashcards.front: The two groups of critical entrepreneurial skills
flashcards.back: Analysis and critical thinking (calculated risk taking, embracing uncertainty, opportunity creation, organization and time management, resource gathering); written and oral communication (storytelling, vision, persuasion and negotiation, decision making, leadership).

flashcards.front: Why studying an industry is the best route to opportunity
flashcards.back: The best opportunities come from experience and knowledge of an industry, and opportunities can be found anywhere along its value chain, not only in products.

flashcards.front: LocalBite's three key concerns
flashcards.back: He thinks he needs a large amount of money; he feels the idea must be completely unique; he has no business experience and fears failure.

flashcards.front: LocalBite's recommended first step
flashcards.back: Test the product with 30–50 customers before investing more money.

flashcards.front: The four pieces of support and advice in the LocalBite case
flashcards.back: Find a mentor; build a network with entrepreneurs and potential customers; study the food industry and develop digital marketing skills; test the market before writing a detailed business plan.

flashcards.front: Which myths LocalBite's worries match
flashcards.back: Money: Myth 1. Unique idea: Myth 2. Fear of failure without experience: Myths 3 and 6. Testing before a detailed plan reflects Myth 4.

flashcards.front: Suggested starting approach for LocalBite
flashcards.back: Start from home and sell through Instagram, TikTok and online marketplaces, using savings of 5 million Indonesian rupiah.

flashcards.front: TAM, SAM and SOM in the LocalBite blueprint
flashcards.back: Total addressable market Rp 848.9 trillion; serviceable available market Rp 394.3 billion; serviceable obtainable market Rp 101.2 million (about 0.026% of SAM), limited by production capacity.

flashcards.front: The blueprint's three-month launch sequence
flashcards.back: Month 1: zero-commission channels (WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok); month 2: delivery apps; month 3 onward: e-commerce and local supermarket consignment. Projected total profit Rp 5,832,000.

flashcards.front: Idea versus opportunity
flashcards.back: Ideas are a commodity everyone has; an opportunity is an idea with commercial potential that can turn into a business. Opportunity is the intersection of an idea and a customer.

flashcards.front: Definition of design thinking
flashcards.back: A process and approach that looks at the world from the customer's perspective, moving from inspiration (creativity) to ideation (opportunity development) to implementation (innovation and commercialization).

flashcards.front: Four things design thinking does
flashcards.back: Define a problem; create and consider multiple options; refine them through iteration; settle on a winning solution.

flashcards.front: The heart of design thinking
flashcards.back: Empathy: a deep understanding of what customers want, gained by embedding in their world.

flashcards.front: Four characteristics of design thinkers besides empathy
flashcards.back: Integrative thinking, optimism, experimentation and collaboration.

flashcards.front: Tools of the innovation/implementation group
flashcards.back: Rapid prototyping, hypothesis testing and launch to learn.

flashcards.front: Questions asked in the opportunity/ideation group
flashcards.back: What is possible? What problem is being solved? Are there customers for a solution?

flashcards.front: Creativity, invention and innovation
flashcards.back: Creativity: using imagination to produce original ideas. Invention: discovering something that did not exist. Innovation: a new way to do something or an improvement to an existing product or service.

flashcards.front: Wallas's four stages of the creative process
flashcards.back: Preparation; incubation; illumination; verification.

flashcards.front: Seeff's seven stages of the creative process
flashcards.back: Hearing the call; fear and resistance; resolution; turning point; creation; manifestation; fulfillment.

flashcards.front: Two types of roadblock to creativity, with an example of each
flashcards.back: Environmental (multitasking lowers productivity) and personal (needing ideas to seem acceptable or rational to others).

flashcards.front: Three actions to build creative confidence
flashcards.back: Set manageable goals for small wins; learn everything about the idea; know when to stop improving and move into action mode.

flashcards.front: Four rules of thumb for generating ideas
flashcards.back: Generate individually first in a group; quantity over quality at first; capture every idea; piggyback on ideas only after individual generation.

flashcards.front: Brainwriting
flashcards.back: Brainstorming in which everyone writes ideas on sticky notes, which are organized into themes and unusual combinations, so all members feel comfortable contributing.

flashcards.front: Journey mapping
flashcards.back: Depicting all touch points a company has with a customer, from awareness of need and purchase through use, service and final disposal.

flashcards.front: The five ways to develop creative skills
flashcards.back: Design a creative environment; log ideas; put the familiar in a new context; use your personal network; visualize something.

flashcards.front: Discovery theory of opportunity
flashcards.back: Opportunities arise from shifts in external factors (regulation, technology, customer preferences); entrepreneurs spot them through alertness.

flashcards.front: Three attributes that make up entrepreneurial alertness
flashcards.back: Risk preference; cognitive differences; information asymmetries.

flashcards.front: Creation theory of opportunity
flashcards.back: Entrepreneurs create opportunities through actions, reactions and experiments; there are no seeds in the market, and any seeds lie within the entrepreneur.

flashcards.front: Affirmative judgment
flashcards.back: Looking for the strengths or positive aspects of a problem first, instead of killing "crazy" ideas quickly.

flashcards.front: Four components of an effective problem statement
flashcards.back: A "how" question; who is responsible for dealing with the problem; an action verb for the positive course of action; the target or desired outcome.

flashcards.front: Final problem statement in the mobile ultrasound device example
flashcards.back: "How can we speed up our product development process?" (reached by asking why five times from "How can we sell more mobile ultrasound devices?").

flashcards.front: Attribute identification versus force fitting
flashcards.back: Attribute identification breaks a problem into elements and modifies each; force fitting applies the characteristics of a random object to the problem.

flashcards.front: Explicit versus implicit criteria for solutions
flashcards.back: Explicit: formal, such as time limits and budgets. Implicit: unstated, such as intuition, team culture, preferences, prejudices and experience-based perspectives.

flashcards.front: Schumpeter's five categories of innovation
flashcards.back: A new product or substantial change; a new process; a new market; new sources of supply; changes in industrial organization.

flashcards.front: Definition of commercialization
flashcards.back: The process that moves an innovation from the laboratory to the market by executing a business strategy.

flashcards.front: Six research areas that start commercialization
flashcards.back: The industry; the target market; intellectual property and regulatory requirements; the customer; the business model; the business design.

flashcards.front: The outcomes and execution decisions of commercialization
flashcards.back: Outcomes: startup capital requirements, revenue sources and cost drivers. Execution: makeup of the management team and market timing.

flashcards.front: Incremental versus disruptive innovation, with examples
flashcards.back: Incremental improves an existing base to differentiate (Apple iPad). Disruptive or radical makes previous technology obsolete (the Internet, the birth control pill, artificial intelligence).

flashcards.front: Eight sources of innovation
flashcards.back: Customers; online news and magazines; observation; demographic shifts; new laws and regulations; emerging industries; trends; business operations.

flashcards.front: Industry versus market
flashcards.back: An industry is defined by a product or service (businesses in a common value chain or channel); a market is defined by customers, those who pay for the benefits.

flashcards.front: Primary market
flashcards.back: The customers with the most need for what the venture offers; identifying it and the first customer is a key feasibility task.

flashcards.front: Two reasons to study the industry
flashcards.back: It is the business's external environment, which no business is independent of; and it shows whether a profit can be made and whether it is worth the effort.

flashcards.front: Gross margin formula and meaning
flashcards.back: Gross profit ÷ sales; it shows how much is left to pay overhead and make a profit, so how much room there is for mistakes.

flashcards.front: Why primary field data are needed after secondary research
flashcards.back: Secondary sources rarely give the most current information because of the lead time from data gathering to print.

flashcards.front: Six sources of primary industry data
flashcards.back: Industry observers and analysts; suppliers and distributors; customers; employees of key firms; professionals from service organizations; trade shows.

flashcards.front: The six stages of the industry life cycle
flashcards.back: Emerging; growth; differentiation; shakeout; maturity; decline.

flashcards.front: What happens in the shakeout stage
flashcards.back: Dominant firms emerge as weaker firms leave.

flashcards.front: The value chain and why it matters
flashcards.back: All companies contributing to the development and distribution of an industry's products; locating the venture on it shows who pays whom and helps set costs and prices.

flashcards.front: Porter's five forces
flashcards.back: Barriers to entry (threat of new entrants); threat of substitutes; buyers' bargaining power; suppliers' bargaining power; rivalry among existing firms.

flashcards.front: Seven barriers to entry
flashcards.back: Economies of scale; brand loyalty; capital requirements; switching costs for the buyer; access to distribution channels; proprietary factors; government regulations.

flashcards.front: Forward integration by suppliers
flashcards.back: Suppliers buying the outlets for their goods and services, so they control the final selling price.

flashcards.front: Three ways suppliers exert power
flashcards.back: Threatening to raise prices; limiting quality or quantity supplied; changing the quality of products supplied (and integrating forward).

flashcards.front: Profile of an attractive industry
flashcards.back: High barriers to entry; weak supplier and buyer power; few substitutes; not highly competitive.

flashcards.front: How a new venture should enter a highly competitive market
flashcards.back: Identify a niche that serves an unmet customer need and enter quietly to gain a foothold, avoiding price wars and costly advertising battles.

flashcards.front: Porter's basic premise
flashcards.back: Sustaining high performance requires a well-thought-out strategy and implementation plan based on how the industry works and how attractive its markets are.

flashcards.front: Three goals of market research for a new company
flashcards.back: Identify and profile the first customer; estimate their potential demand; identify subsequent segments for growth.

flashcards.front: The first customer
flashcards.back: The customer with a significant problem the venture can solve; often an unserved niche rather than the biggest market.

flashcards.front: The four-step process for gathering market data
flashcards.back: Assess information needs; research secondary sources first; measure the target market with primary research; forecast demand.

flashcards.front: The customer discovery hierarchy
flashcards.back: Gatekeepers (control access and information); influencers (approval often required); deciders (final decision, usually on budget); purchasers (authority to buy); users (ultimate beneficiaries).

flashcards.front: Four ways to collect primary customer data
flashcards.back: Ethnographic observation; interviews; informal focus groups; online or in-person surveys.

flashcards.front: Five steps of the ethnographic approach for entrepreneurs
flashcards.back: Learn from observation; explain what was observed; develop a hypothesis; test the theory; draw conclusions.

flashcards.front: Five advantages of personal interviews
flashcards.back: More clarification and discussion; nonverbal cues show truthfulness; high response rate; open-ended questions for depth; networking and contacts.

flashcards.front: Four rules for questionnaire design
flashcards.back: Keep it short with white space; no leading or biased questions; easy questions first; demographic questions last.

flashcards.front: Why survey samples should be random
flashcards.back: To avoid bias: the researcher should have as little control as possible over who is selected.

flashcards.front: What a customer matrix lays out for each segment
flashcards.back: Pain, benefit, distribution channel, product or service and potential competition.

flashcards.front: Six items in a customer profile
flashcards.back: Age; income level; education; buying habits (when, where, how much); where they find such products; how they would like to buy them.

flashcards.front: Why demand questions should seek outcomes
flashcards.back: Customers describe problems and desired outcomes well but solutions poorly, so outcome questions lead to better solution design.

flashcards.front: Four reasons entrepreneurs underestimate competition
flashcards.back: Incomplete information; underestimating resources and skills needed; missing roadblocks; not knowing what they do not know.

flashcards.front: Three types of competitor
flashcards.back: Direct (same needs, same resources); indirect or substitute (same needs, different resources or channels); emerging or potential (could move in quickly).

flashcards.front: Good versus bad competition
flashcards.back: Good: competitors performing badly with unhappy customers, an opening. Bad: competitors doing everything right with happy customers, hard to displace.

flashcards.front: Three checks for threats from outside the industry
flashcards.back: What the competitor must do to succeed in its core business; whether it has a competency in your area; which core competencies transfer to your business.

flashcards.front: Four ways to find competitor information
flashcards.back: Visit websites and outlets; buy their products; read customer comments online; use Hoover's Online, the Securities and Exchange Commission and OneSource for public companies.

flashcards.front: Drucker's five business model questions
flashcards.back: What is our mission? Who is our customer? What does our customer value? What are our results? What is our plan?

flashcards.front: The essence of a business model
flashcards.back: The strategic decisions and trade-offs entrepreneurs make to earn a profit (also described as a blueprint or an analytical device for evaluation and action).

flashcards.front: Value proposition
flashcards.back: The benefit the customer derives, the reason they will buy: the unique mix of product, price, service, relationship and image, explaining what the company does better or differently.

flashcards.front: Features versus benefits
flashcards.back: Benefits are intangibles (better health, saving time and money, reliability); features are product attributes (design, physical characteristics, functions).

flashcards.front: Segmenting a market
flashcards.back: Dividing it into meaningful and measurable parts based on needs, buyer behaviors and demographics.

flashcards.front: Three advantages of selling direct to the customer
flashcards.back: Large upside potential; control over branding, pricing and relationship; management of user data and experience.

flashcards.front: Three advantages of selling through an intermediary
flashcards.back: Partner does the build-out and capital investment; partner handles billing and service; more predictable cash flow with a licensing agreement.

flashcards.front: The most common type of strategic partnership
flashcards.back: The buyer–supplier relationship, used to cut costs or share facilities such as manufacturing or warehousing.

flashcards.front: The blocks of the entrepreneur's business model canvas
flashcards.back: Problem; solution; key metrics; unique value proposition; unfair advantage; channels and strategic partners; customer segments; cost structure; revenue streams.

flashcards.front: Five revenue models
flashcards.back: Subscription or membership; volume or unit-based; licensing and syndication; transaction fee; advertising.

flashcards.front: What makes a revenue model healthy
flashcards.back: Revenue from multiple types of customers and multiple products and services.

flashcards.front: Three kinds of cost driver
flashcards.back: Fixed (rent), variable (manufacturing), nonrecurring (one-time expense).

flashcards.front: Five cost structures
flashcards.back: Marketing or advertising; inventory; office or retail space; support center; direct cost structure.

flashcards.front: Cost-driven versus value-driven model
flashcards.back: Cost-driven keeps costs as low as possible because margins are narrow; value-driven creates premium experiences with personalized service and luxury facilities.

flashcards.front: Five ways business models change
flashcards.back: Incremental expansion (geography, markets, pricing, lines, channels); revitalizing an established model; taking a model into new areas; adding models by acquisition; building new models on core competencies.

flashcards.front: Break-even units formula
flashcards.back: Fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit).

flashcards.front: Definition of feasibility analysis
flashcards.back: The testing, evaluation and validation of a proposed business model for a new venture; a tool to assess and reduce risk at startup.

flashcards.front: Four things to understand when assessing an opportunity
flashcards.back: Your capabilities; competitors' capabilities and intentions; customers' needs and desires; your bargaining power in the value chain.

flashcards.front: The four areas of feasibility analysis
flashcards.back: Industry and market/customer; product/service; founding team; financial needs assessment.

flashcards.front: Six steps to validate a business model
flashcards.back: Develop hypotheses for each component; design an experiment for each; test with customers in the field; consider the impact on all components; change the model; retest until fully validated.

flashcards.front: Three critical success factors tested in feasibility analysis
flashcards.back: Is the market big enough to be viable and grow? Do capital requirements to reach positive cash flow make sense? Can an appropriate founding team be assembled?

flashcards.front: Three groups of macro environmental factors
flashcards.back: Industry factors and trends; market factors and trends; global economic factors.

flashcards.front: Taleb's antifragile business
flashcards.back: One that guards what it cannot afford to lose (about 90 percent) and takes risks with about 10 percent, benefiting from positive uncertainty without suffering the negative side.

flashcards.front: The waiting-in-line app's initial unvalidated model
flashcards.back: Value proposition: save time, avoid lines; segment: students; channel: direct; partners: concession stands, food trucks; revenue: advertising and partner subscriptions; costs: software development, sales force.

flashcards.front: Blue ocean strategy
flashcards.back: Kim and Mauborgne's idea of seeking white spaces where no one is playing, at the intersection of value and cost.

flashcards.front: The four blue ocean actions
flashcards.back: Eliminate something the industry has always done; reduce something below the standard; raise something above the standard; create something the industry has never done.

flashcards.front: Two contexts with challenging business models
flashcards.back: Where the customer does not want to pay, and where the startup faces dominant players.

flashcards.front: Three ways to monetize a platform whose users will not pay
flashcards.back: Advertising (under attack from advertisers and users); freemium (basic free, paid enhanced features); sponsorship (an entity funds free access).

flashcards.front: Two-sided platform
flashcards.back: A platform acting as intermediary where users upload and share content and so become the content providers who add to its value.

flashcards.front: How startups facing dominant players often compete
flashcards.back: By acquiring intellectual property and know-how they control and developing it until it is attractive to a dominant firm.

flashcards.front: FreshMart's main business model
flashcards.back: A store-based omnichannel reseller living on margin: buy well (bulk, own brand), place stock close to demand (25 stores, three channels), sell volume.

flashcards.front: FreshMart's three problems
flashcards.back: High delivery cost on small orders; unsold fresh food; customers switching for discounts.

flashcards.front: FreshMart's value proposition versus business model
flashcards.back: Value proposition (the promise): affordable, close and convenient, rewarding. Business model (the machine): purchasing creates, channels deliver, revenue captures value.

flashcards.front: Target segment chosen in the FreshMart analysis, and why
flashcards.back: Young working adults: steadier income, they buy time rather than discounts, and the case names their need for ready-to-eat meals.

flashcards.front: Break-even delivery basket at FreshMart
flashcards.back: Rp 12,000 per trip ÷ 25% gross margin = Rp 48,000; smaller delivered orders lose money.

flashcards.front: FreshMart Plus offer
flashcards.back: Rp 29,000 a month; free 30-minute delivery on orders from Rp 75,000 within about 3 km; member meal prices; double points on own brand; non-members pay delivery, minimum Rp 50,000.

flashcards.front: The biggest risk of FreshMart Plus and its effect
flashcards.back: Members move store trips into free delivery: a Rp 100,000 basket earns Rp 25,000 walked in but Rp 13,000 delivered, so profit roughly halves.

flashcards.front: FreshMart Plus test plan
flashcards.back: Weeks 1–2 fake-door test; weeks 3–10 pilot in 2 stores with 2 control stores; week 11 decide to scale, adjust or stop.

flashcards.front: Goal of the product development process
flashcards.back: Bring new products to market at the right time and cost, so customers pay a price reflecting the value they perceive.

flashcards.front: Definition of product design
flashcards.back: The activity that transforms a set of requirements into an integrated whole or system.

flashcards.front: The seven elements of the product design system
flashcards.back: Form; texture; color; fit; user interfaces; production and assembly processes; methods for joining the parts.

flashcards.front: Share of final cost determined by design
flashcards.back: As much as 80 percent.

flashcards.front: Failure rate of new consumer products, and the principal reason
flashcards.back: Between 70 and 90 percent; the principal reason is lack of good market and industry analysis.

flashcards.front: Creating versus capturing value
flashcards.back: Innovators may create value for customers but, unless they capture enough that customers will pay for, imitators and complementary providers take the returns.

flashcards.front: Industry architecture as a cause of failure
flashcards.back: Firms that offer only part of a solution (system integrators, such as independent film studios) may see the product earn money while they do not, because they do not own content or proprietary technology.

flashcards.front: Five problems caused by too few new product development resources
flashcards.back: Poor execution; longer time to market; missed first-to-market opportunities; projects simplified; declining team morale.

flashcards.front: The three categories of the product development cycle and their questions
flashcards.back: Customer identification or discovery (who is the customer, what do they need?); customer validation and design (how to design, develop and test product, market and model?); business creation (what launch strategy?).

flashcards.front: The eight product development tasks
flashcards.back: Discovery; opportunity recognition; feasibility; intellectual property and regulatory requirements; prototype development; market and customer tests; launch strategy; execution plan.

flashcards.front: Six questions when validating a solution
flashcards.back: Does it already exist? Does it solve the problem? Can it be produced? Can it be protected? What will it cost? How long to market?

flashcards.front: Four sections of the new product checklist
flashcards.back: The market; strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats; design, development and manufacturing; financial.

flashcards.front: Three uses of physical prototypes
flashcards.back: Communicate form, fit and function to customers; give a vendor an example to quote on; allow quick design changes.

flashcards.front: Prototypes for non-manufacturing businesses
flashcards.back: A design, storyboard or flowchart of how the business will deliver its service or product.

flashcards.front: Four ways to commercialize a technology
flashcards.back: License it; start a business to make and distribute it; sell it; form a joint venture with a company that has the resources.

flashcards.front: Five factors traded off in product development
flashcards.back: Product features; cost; capital expenditures; development costs; timing.

flashcards.front: Features versus product cost trade-off advice
flashcards.back: Put most product cost into the features that matter most to customers and cut features that add no value.

flashcards.front: Definition of a minimum viable product (MVP)
flashcards.back: The version of a product with just enough functionality and value proposition to attract early adopters who give feedback and help develop the final mass-market product.

flashcards.front: Goal of the MVP versus goal of the final product
flashcards.back: MVP: attract initial customers who guide the product. Final product: attract passionate users who refer it to others.

flashcards.front: MVP approach at the incremental end of the innovation spectrum
flashcards.back: Customers have real problems and alternatives from major players, so build more than a simple MVP; a complete product may make more sense.

flashcards.front: MVP approach at the disruptive end of the innovation spectrum
flashcards.back: No direct competition and customers forgive flaws, so build the MVP in stages based on customer feedback.

flashcards.front: What produces a viable product, according to the slides
flashcards.back: Not the number of MVP iterations, but how well you recognize when customers tell you the product is viable.

flashcards.front: Gains from outsourcing product development
flashcards.back: Risk, cost and cycle time can fall by 60 to 90 percent, plus access to a network of expertise a young firm could not afford.

flashcards.front: Three rules of thumb for development service firms
flashcards.back: Do not give design and development to the same firm unless it specializes in both; spend enough time on design before building; break development into parts for cheap early tests.

flashcards.front: Four cautions on outsourcing
flashcards.back: Never choose on price alone; keep core research and development close to the customer; distance management is harder and costlier; intellectual property is hard to protect where piracy is rampant.

flashcards.front: Three categories of knowledge
flashcards.back: Intellectual capital (tacit knowledge from daily work); intellectual assets (explicit, documented knowledge); intellectual property (exclusive legal rights).

flashcards.front: Four examples of intellectual property every business has
flashcards.back: A trademark on its name or brand; copyrights on advertising design; patents on an invented device; trade secrets such as the customer list.

flashcards.front: How intellectual property resembles and differs from personal property
flashcards.back: Like property, it can be bought, sold, donated, licensed or exchanged and must be defended; unlike it, it is intangible, a right under law that must be put into physical form to be exercised.

flashcards.front: The intellectual property pyramid from least to most protection
flashcards.back: Trade secrets; copyrights; trademarks; patents.

flashcards.front: Trade secret definition (Uniform Trade Secrets Act)
flashcards.back: A formula, device, idea, process, pattern or compilation of information that gives a competitive advantage, is not common knowledge, and is kept reasonably confidential.

flashcards.front: Five examples of trade secrets
flashcards.back: Pollsters' survey methods; customer lists; source codes for computer chips; customer discounts; inventions that will not be patented.

flashcards.front: How trade secrets are protected, and the remedies
flashcards.back: Only by confidentiality agreements or contracts; remedies are injunctive relief, damages and attorney's fees, within a statute of limitations that varies by state.

flashcards.front: Definition of a trademark, with three examples
flashcards.back: A symbol, logo, word, sound, color, design or other device identifying a business or product in commerce: FedEx logo, L'Oréal "Because you're worth it," Coca-Cola bottle shape.

flashcards.front: When a color can be trademarked
flashcards.back: When it has secondary meaning (people associate it with a specific product, such as pink insulation); a logo's background color alone cannot be.

flashcards.front: How long a trademark lasts, and how it is lost
flashcards.back: As long as it is actively used and renewal fees are paid; lost if it becomes generic (aspirin, thermos).

flashcards.front: Three kinds of mark that cannot be trademarked
flashcards.back: Immoral or deceptive marks; official symbols such as flags; a person's name or likeness without permission.

flashcards.front: Trademark dilution versus counterfeiting
flashcards.back: Dilution: the mark's value is substantially reduced through competition or likely confusion. Counterfeiting: deliberate copying, subject to civil and criminal penalties.

flashcards.front: Four steps to register a trademark
flashcards.back: Search existing marks; pick a mark that is not common or closely descriptive; test its translation in target languages; choose product and service categories.

flashcards.front: Six rights of a copyright owner (as taught)
flashcards.back: Reproduction; derivative works; distribution; public performance; public display; digital transmission performance.

flashcards.front: Copyright terms taught in the course
flashcards.back: Life of the copyright holder plus 70 years (Copyright Extension Act of 1998); works for hire and anonymous works 95 years from publication; Berne Convention minimum life of the author plus 50 years.

flashcards.front: Doctrine of Fair Use
flashcards.back: Reproduction is "fair" for criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship and research.

flashcards.front: Digital Millennium Copyright Act (1998)
flashcards.back: Bans falsifying or removing copyright management data and circumventing encryption, and making tools to do so; a safe harbor protects Internet service providers that infringe unknowingly.

flashcards.front: Three parts of a copyright notice
flashcards.back: The word "copyright" or ©; the year of first publication; the owner's full name.

flashcards.front: What a patent gives its holder
flashcards.back: The exclusionary right to stop others making, using, offering for sale or selling the invention, usually for 20 years from application; then it enters the public domain.

flashcards.front: Four signals that a patent may be needed
flashcards.back: Solves a significant problem and changes how things are done; falls under Food and Drug Administration regulation; revenues exceed enforcement cost; a plan to license it.

flashcards.front: Economic life and the patent decision
flashcards.back: The period the invention can generate revenue; in fast-changing fields a patent may outlive it, but for long, regulated development patents are essential.

flashcards.front: Four criteria for patentability
flashcards.back: Fits a statutory class; has utility; is novel (no prior art); is not obvious to someone of ordinary skill.

flashcards.front: The four statutory classes
flashcards.back: Machine; process or method; article of manufacture; composition of matter.

flashcards.front: Three patent types and their terms (as taught)
flashcards.back: Utility: 20 years from application. Plant: 20 years from filing. Design: 14 years from issuance (15 years from grant for applications since May 2015).

flashcards.front: Provisional patent application
flashcards.back: A lower-cost first filing allowing "patent pending" for 12 months (no extension); the nonprovisional must follow, and the 12 months do not count toward the 20-year term.

flashcards.front: Effect of the America Invents Act
flashcards.back: The United States became first-inventor-to-file: the filing date, not the date of conception, decides between two inventors.

flashcards.front: Patent publication and maintenance timing
flashcards.back: Most applications are published 18 months after filing; maintenance fees are due 3½, 7½ and 11½ years after grant.

flashcards.front: Doctrine of equivalents
flashcards.back: Protects inventors against infringers who make small, insignificant changes to the claims.

flashcards.front: Why patents are the most time-sensitive form of protection
flashcards.back: Under first-to-file, the longer an entrepreneur waits, the greater the chance the invention is no longer novel.

flashcards.front: Who wins a trademark dispute under intent-to-use filing
flashcards.back: Usually the party with the earliest intent-to-use filing date; the first to file holds the presumptive right.

flashcards.front: Three patent strategies
flashcards.back: Proprietary (acquire patents to cover the opportunity and defend position); defensive (design around patents or build a portfolio for cross-licensing); leveraging (when freedom to operate or proprietary protection is not critical).

flashcards.front: Reach of a United States patent
flashcards.back: Only within United States borders; it has no effect in any foreign country.

flashcards.front: Patent Cooperation Treaty deadlines
flashcards.back: File the international application within 12 months of the first filing to keep that date; enter the national phase in chosen countries within 30 months.

flashcards.front: How a trademark is protected abroad
flashcards.back: Register in each target market (the home registration helps), test the mark's translation, and record it with customs to block counterfeit imports.

flashcards.front: The seven-step answer chain for a case question
flashcards.back: Opportunity; industry and market; business model; feasibility; prototype or MVP; protect; recommend.

flashcards.front: Two habits that lift a case answer from adequate to excellent
flashcards.back: Quantifying with case numbers or calculations, and sequencing the recommendation with a reason for the order.

flashcards.front: The recurring message of the course
flashcards.back: Test before you scale: a model that works at home is only a hypothesis abroad.

flashcards.front: Sequencing examples from the three cases
flashcards.back: EuroDisney: cash, then product, then reinvestment. FreshMart: 2 stores before 25. LocalBite: 30–50 customers before a detailed plan.

flashcards.front: Factors that change a business model abroad
flashcards.back: Culture, climate, income and leisure budgets, holiday patterns, language and law.

flashcards.front: How to open a decision answer
flashcards.back: Answer the question directly in the first two lines ("Yes, but only after…"), then build the framework chain.

flashcards.front: 3D
flashcards.back: Three-dimensional: used of printing technology and of physical prototypes

flashcards.front: AI
flashcards.back: Artificial intelligence: machine-learning solutions that complete specific tasks and augment human decisions

flashcards.front: AIA
flashcards.back: America Invents Act: United States law that made the country first-inventor-to-file (effective 16 March 2013)

flashcards.front: B2B
flashcards.back: Business-to-business: sales to organizations rather than consumers

flashcards.front: BINUS
flashcards.back: Bina Nusantara: the university running the course (BINUS University, BINUS Higher Education)

flashcards.front: BPOM
flashcards.back: Badan Pengawas Obat dan Makanan: Indonesia's food and drug authority, which registers packaged food

flashcards.front: BRIC
flashcards.back: Brazil, Russia, India and China: large emerging economies

flashcards.front: CEO
flashcards.back: Chief executive officer

flashcards.front: CGT
flashcards.back: Confédération Générale du Travail: the communist-led French labor federation in the EuroDisneyland case

flashcards.front: CILO
flashcards.back: Course intended learning outcome: CILO 1 identify international market opportunities and the business environment; CILO 2 analyze a business model and strategic plan for international expansion

flashcards.front: COGS
flashcards.back: Cost of goods sold: the direct cost of producing what is sold

flashcards.front: CRISPR
flashcards.back: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats: a gene-editing technology for changing the genome of living cells

flashcards.front: DC
flashcards.back: District of Columbia: Washington, DC, home of the Copyright Office of the Library of Congress

flashcards.front: DMCA
flashcards.back: Digital Millennium Copyright Act (1998): bans removing copyright management data and circumventing encryption; safe harbor for Internet service providers

flashcards.front: FDA
flashcards.back: Food and Drug Administration: the United States regulator of food, drugs and medical devices

flashcards.front: FFr
flashcards.back: French francs: France's currency before the euro, used in the EuroDisneyland case

flashcards.front: GEM
flashcards.back: Global Entrepreneurship Monitor: annual study that groups countries as factor-, efficiency- or innovation-driven economies

flashcards.front: IDR
flashcards.back: Indonesian rupiah (currency code); also written Rp

flashcards.front: IEEE
flashcards.back: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers: publisher of the systematic review on cultural-based product business models

flashcards.front: IoT
flashcards.back: Internet of Things: everyday devices connected to the Internet

flashcards.front: IP
flashcards.back: Intellectual property: legally protected intangible assets (trade secrets, copyrights, trademarks, patents)

flashcards.front: MVP
flashcards.back: Minimum viable product: the version with just enough functionality and value to attract early adopters who give feedback

flashcards.front: NPD
flashcards.back: New product development

flashcards.front: PCT
flashcards.back: Patent Cooperation Treaty: lets one international application cover all member countries; file within 12 months of the first filing, national phase by month 30

flashcards.front: PIRT
flashcards.back: Pangan Industri Rumah Tangga: Indonesian permit for home-industry food production

flashcards.front: PO
flashcards.back: Pre-order: an order placed and usually paid before the product is made

flashcards.front: PTAB
flashcards.back: Patent Trial and Appeal Board: the USPTO appeal body since 2012, replacing the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences

flashcards.front: R&D
flashcards.back: Research and development

flashcards.front: Rp
flashcards.back: Rupiah: Indonesian currency (code IDR)

flashcards.front: SAM
flashcards.back: Serviceable available market: the part of the total market the venture can reach

flashcards.front: SBA
flashcards.back: Small Business Administration: United States agency that reported 52 percent of small businesses were home-based (2014)

flashcards.front: SEC
flashcards.back: Securities and Exchange Commission: United States regulator whose filings give information on public companies

flashcards.front: SKU
flashcards.back: Stock-keeping unit: one distinct product variant held in stock

flashcards.front: SM
flashcards.back: Service mark: symbol used after a service brand before it is registered

flashcards.front: SOM
flashcards.back: Serviceable obtainable market: the share of the serviceable market the venture can realistically win

flashcards.front: SWOT
flashcards.back: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats

flashcards.front: TAM
flashcards.back: Total addressable market: total demand for the product category

flashcards.front: TM
flashcards.back: Trademark: symbol used after a brand before it is registered (® after registration)

flashcards.front: USPTO
flashcards.back: United States Patent and Trademark Office

flashcards.front: VAT
flashcards.back: Value added tax: cut from 18.6% to 7% on EuroDisneyland tickets

flashcards.front: WIPO
flashcards.back: World Intellectual Property Organization: the United Nations agency that administers the PCT

quiz.q: Which pair of weeks serves CILO 2 (analyzing a business model and strategic plan for international expansion)?
quiz.why: Weeks 1–5 serve CILO 1; Prototyping and Validation (Week 6) and Legal Consideration and Asset Protection Abroad (Week 7) serve CILO 2.

quiz.q: Which case is set beside Week 5 to test business model concepts?
quiz.why: FreshMart asks students to separate business model from value proposition and choose a model change. Astro is only a benchmark inside the FreshMart analysis.

quiz.q: In Stevenson's definition, entrepreneurs pursue opportunities…
options: only after securing the resources they need
only when working on their own
without regard to the resources they currently control
quiz.why: The definition stresses opportunity first and resources second, and it covers people working alone or inside organizations.

quiz.q: In which phase of the entrepreneurial process are hypotheses about the customer, solution and business model tested?
quiz.why: Phase 1 forms the hypotheses; Phase 2 validates them and reveals revenue sources and cost drivers; Phase 3 designs and plans execution.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the environmental variables the slides say a new venture keeps responding to?
quiz.why: The five variables are the economy, competition, new laws and regulations, labor supply and sources of capital. Brand loyalty is a barrier to entry in Porter's model.

quiz.q: Technological change happens when an entrepreneur identifies all of the following EXCEPT…
options: new customer segments that appear to be emerging
existing customer needs that have not been satisfied
new ways of manufacturing and distributing
quiz.why: The four signals are customer-side: emerging segments, new needs, unsatisfied needs and new ways to make and distribute.

quiz.q: In which Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) economy type are businesses most often created out of necessity?
quiz.why: Factor-driven economies rely on unskilled labor and natural resources, so necessity drives very high entrepreneurial activity. "Knowledge-driven" is not a GEM category.

quiz.q: A venture that creates jobs not drawn from existing businesses and serves currently unserved needs shows which high-impact trait?
quiz.why: Value-creating is defined by new jobs that do not draw from existing firms and by serving unserved needs; innovative means bringing something new, growth-oriented means regional to global ambition.

quiz.q: What is the "fuzzy front end"?
options: The first year after launch, when cash flow is uncertain
The period before launch, when activities are unclear and change as information arrives
The decline stage of the industry life cycle
The point at which investors join the venture
quiz.why: The fuzzy front end precedes launch and startup; it is where much new venture risk sits.

quiz.q: A founder builds an app nobody asked for and no customer will pay for. Which failure reason is this?
options: A solution looking for a problem
Poor communication of the value proposition
quiz.why: A "me-too" solution copies what exists; here there is no real need at all, which is the first failure reason.

quiz.q: According to the slides, when did the word "entrepreneur" come into popular use in the United States?
quiz.why: The 1980s are called the decade of entrepreneurship; the 1960s were "bigger is better."

quiz.q: EuroDisneyland drew about 10 million visitors, above its 7–8 million break-even, yet lost money. The best explanation is that…
options: attendance fell short of the break-even in the first year
Disney took no royalties from the park
the break-even was set for the $1 billion plan and never updated as costs rose to $4.4 billion
the French government withdrew its loans
quiz.why: Attendance exceeded the stated break-even, so the stale break-even calculation is the key; Disney did take royalties, and the loans were provided.

quiz.q: EuroDisney's spend-to-admission ratio was about 0.80×, against Tokyo's 2.04×. What does this show?
options: EuroDisney charged the lowest ticket of all Disney parks
Visitors paid the highest ticket but spent the least in total
Tokyo visitors paid more for admission than EuroDisney visitors
EuroDisney's visitors spent more on food than on tickets
quiz.why: Adult tickets: EuroDisney $47, Tokyo $38; total spend EuroDisney $30–45, Tokyo $70–85.

quiz.q: Why could Disney earn money from EuroDisneyland while other shareholders lost money?
options: Its royalties and management fees were charged on revenue, not profit
It sold its stake before opening
French law guaranteed Disney a minimum profit
quiz.why: Disney held 49%, and its 10% admission and 5% food and merchandise royalties plus fees came off revenue.

quiz.q: What do the slides say research has found about the "typical entrepreneur"?
options: Most successful entrepreneurs share a high tolerance for risk
Successful entrepreneurs usually come from business families
No psychological or sociological traits predict with certainty who will become or succeed as an entrepreneur
quiz.why: Research has failed to identify a stereotypical entrepreneur; the other options are exactly the stereotypes the week dismisses.

quiz.q: A founder says: "I cannot start until I have a perfect, formal business plan." Which myth is this, and what is the current thinking?
options: Myth 1: raise more money before planning
Myth 3: take bigger risks for bigger rewards
Myth 4: first get in front of customers to test the idea, then have a plan to grow
Myth 6: hire someone who already knows entrepreneurship
quiz.why: Myth 4 says a plan is required for success; the slides say test with customers first, then plan for growth.

quiz.q: Peter Drucker is quoted against which myth?
options: It takes a lot of money to start a business
Entrepreneurship is for the young and reckless
The bigger the risk, the bigger the reward
quiz.why: Drucker: "It is a discipline. And, like any discipline, it can be learned."

quiz.q: A company assigns ownership of a new business idea to a manager and gives modest seed funding to test it. Which corporate entrepreneurship model is this?
quiz.why: The advocate acts as evangelist with ownership and modest seed money; the producer sets up a formal unit with dedicated funds and autonomy.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a portfolio entrepreneur from a serial entrepreneur?
options: A portfolio entrepreneur only invests and never manages
A serial entrepreneur runs several businesses at the same time
A serial entrepreneur only works inside corporations
A portfolio entrepreneur holds stakes in several ventures at once
quiz.why: Serial entrepreneurs start one business after another; portfolio entrepreneurs own minority or majority stakes in several ventures simultaneously.

quiz.q: Which statement about nonprofit ventures matches the slides?
options: They are not allowed to make any profit
Their profit is distributed to donors
They can and should make a profit, but the profit stays in the organization
quiz.why: Contrary to popular belief, nonprofits can profit; the profit is retained, not distributed to owners.

quiz.q: Why do entrepreneurs rely on weak ties for advice?
options: Weak ties are usually wealthier than strong ties
Weak ties are not biased by a prior history with the entrepreneur, so their advice is more objective
Strong ties refuse to give advice
Weak ties are bound by confidentiality agreements
quiz.why: Weak ties (acquaintances, contacts) offer objective advice that helps entrepreneurs move faster; strong ties share a history that colors their view.

quiz.q: In networking, what is a broker?
options: An opinion leader who acts as a gateway between groups or networks
A close family member who funds the venture
A lawyer who drafts partnership agreements
An investor who buys shares in the venture
quiz.why: Brokers exert influence between networks and connect the entrepreneur to new ones.

quiz.q: Which is one of the six barriers that keep people from becoming self-employed?
quiz.why: The six barriers: lack of confidence, financial needs, startup logistics, personal or family issues, time constraints and lack of skills.

quiz.q: What does the LocalBite case recommend as the first step?
options: Write a detailed business plan before selling anything
Raise a large amount of capital from investors
Test the product with 30–50 customers before investing more money
Develop a completely unique snack before launching
quiz.why: The case recommends a small market test first; the other options repeat the founder's myths.

quiz.q: The LocalBite founder believes his idea must be completely unique. Which Week 2 lesson answers this?
options: Unique ideas reduce the need for customers
Execution, usually led by a strong team, matters more than a great idea
quiz.why: Myth 2: great businesses usually started with a great team and an execution plan, not a great idea.

quiz.q: In the LocalBite blueprint, why is the serviceable obtainable market (SOM) only about 0.026% of the serviceable available market (SAM)?
options: It is limited by the solo founder's production capacity, not by demand
Demand for snacks in Bandung is very low
Delivery apps refuse to list the product
The product is sold only to high school students
quiz.why: The blueprint states that capacity, not demand, sets the SOM of Rp 101.2 million.

quiz.q: According to the course, what turns an idea into an opportunity?
options: Writing it down in a journal
Sharing it with friends and family
Matching it to a customer, so it has commercial potential
quiz.why: Opportunity is the intersection of an idea and a customer; ideas alone are a commodity.

quiz.q: What is at the heart of design thinking?
quiz.why: Design thinking requires embedding in the customer's world to see needs from their perspective.

quiz.q: Rapid prototyping and hypothesis testing belong to which group of design thinking activity?
quiz.why: Implementation asks how we know and how we can test; its tools are rapid prototyping, hypothesis testing and launch to learn.

quiz.q: In Wallas's model, which stage involves letting the problem lie in the subconscious?
quiz.why: Preparation views the problem from many angles; incubation lets it rest; illumination finds the solution; verification brings it to an outcome.

quiz.q: When generating ideas in a group, the slides advise that you should…
options: judge each idea for quality as it is suggested
discard outlandish ideas early to save time
generate ideas individually first, then combine them
quiz.why: The rules are individual first, quantity over quality, capture everything, and piggyback only after individual generation.

quiz.q: Which tool depicts all touch points a company has with a customer, from purchase to end of product life?
quiz.why: Journey mapping traces touch points from awareness of need to final disposal.

quiz.q: Creation theory holds that opportunities…
options: arise from shifts in regulation and technology
are created by the entrepreneur's own actions and experiments
are found by reading industry reports
quiz.why: Discovery theory points to external shifts; creation theory says any seeds lie within the entrepreneur.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four components of an effective problem statement?
quiz.why: The four are a how question, who is responsible, an action verb and the target outcome. A budget is a solution criterion.

quiz.q: Intuition, team culture and preferences used to judge solutions are examples of…
quiz.why: Explicit criteria are formal (time limits, budgets); implicit ones are known but unstated.

quiz.q: Which of these is one of Schumpeter's five categories of innovation?
quiz.why: Schumpeter: new product, new process, new market, new sources of supply and changes in industrial organization.

quiz.q: The slides give the Apple iPad as an example of…
quiz.why: The iPad improved on an existing product base; the Internet and artificial intelligence are the disruptive examples.

quiz.q: Commercialization research guides which two critical execution decisions?
options: The makeup of the management team and market timing
The office location and dress code
The share price and dividend policy
quiz.why: Research outcomes drive capital needs, revenue sources and cost drivers; execution decisions are team and timing.

quiz.q: How does the course distinguish an industry from a market?
options: An industry is local; a market is global
An industry includes only manufacturers; a market includes only retailers
They are two names for the same thing
An industry is defined by a product or service; a market is defined by customers who pay for its benefits
quiz.why: Industry analysis looks at businesses in a value chain; market research looks at the customers.

quiz.q: A retailer buys an item at $10 and sells it at $19.95. What is its gross margin?
quiz.why: Gross margin = gross profit ÷ sales = $9.95 ÷ $19.95 ≈ 49.9%. Dividing by cost (99.5%) gives the markup, and 50.1% is the cost share of the price; both are common mistakes.

quiz.q: In which life-cycle stage do dominant firms emerge as weaker firms leave?
quiz.why: Emerging has many entrants and no dominant players; shakeout is where dominance appears; decline has falling demand.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the barriers to entry listed in the slides?
quiz.why: Substitutes are a separate force; the seven barriers are scale, brand loyalty, capital, switching costs, distribution access, proprietary factors and regulation.

quiz.q: A supplier buys the shops that sell its goods to control final prices. This is…
quiz.why: Suppliers integrating forward purchase their outlets and so control the prices at which output is sold.

quiz.q: Which profile describes an attractive industry under the five forces?
options: Low entry barriers, strong buyers, many substitutes
High entry barriers, weak buyer and supplier power, few substitutes, mild rivalry
quiz.why: An attractive industry protects profit potential on every force; the other options describe unattractive features.

quiz.q: In the customer discovery hierarchy, who makes the final purchase decision, usually based on a budget?
quiz.why: Gatekeepers control access, influencers affect the decision, deciders make it, purchasers buy and users benefit.

quiz.q: Which questionnaire practice do the slides recommend?
options: Use leading questions to save time
Make the questionnaire long and detailed
quiz.why: Keep it short, avoid leading questions, start easy and put demographics last when attention may have waned.

quiz.q: Why might the first customer NOT be the biggest potential market?
options: Large markets never buy new products
The first customer is always a government agency
Large markets are illegal to target first
It may be an unserved niche that allows entry without direct competition for a time
quiz.why: The first customer has a significant problem the venture can solve, often in an unserved niche.

quiz.q: A firm not serving your customers today, but with the resources to move in quickly, is…
quiz.why: Direct competitors use the same resources for the same need; indirect ones use different resources; emerging ones could enter fast.

quiz.q: "Good competition" in the course means competitors that…
options: perform badly and leave customers unhappy
quiz.why: Good competition is an opening; bad competition is firms doing everything right with happy customers.

quiz.q: Why should demand questions ask about outcomes rather than solutions?
options: Customers describe problems and desired outcomes well but solutions poorly
Customers refuse to talk about problems
Solutions questions are illegal in surveys
quiz.why: Outcome questions ("How do you want to use…?") lead to better solution design and better demand data.

quiz.q: Which is one of Drucker's five business model questions?
quiz.why: The five: mission, customer, what the customer values, results and plan.

quiz.q: "Saves two hours a week" is an example of a…
quiz.why: Benefits are intangibles such as saving time or money; features are product attributes like design or functions.

quiz.q: Which is an advantage of selling through an intermediary rather than direct?
options: The entrepreneur controls branding and pricing
The partner does the build-out and capital investment
The entrepreneur owns the user data
The entrepreneur keeps the full upside
quiz.why: Going indirect shifts investment, billing and service to the partner but gives up upside, control and data.

quiz.q: A software firm charges users a monthly fee for access. Which revenue model is this?
quiz.why: A recurring access fee is subscription; per-unit sales are volume-based; a charge per transaction is a transaction fee.

quiz.q: Rent is an example of which kind of cost?
quiz.why: The slides give rent as fixed, manufacturing as variable and one-time expenses as nonrecurring.

quiz.q: A business offering personalized service and luxury facilities follows a…
quiz.why: Value-driven models create premium experiences; cost-driven models keep costs low because margins are narrow.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three critical success factors tested in feasibility analysis?
options: Whether the market is large enough to be viable and grow
Whether the founder has a registered patent
Whether capital requirements to reach positive cash flow make sense
Whether an appropriate founding team can be assembled
quiz.why: The three are market, capital and team; patents are a product and intellectual property question.

quiz.q: In Taleb's barbell, an antifragile business…
options: guards about 90 percent of the business and takes risks with about 10 percent
takes large risks with the whole business
splits the business evenly between safe and risky activities
quiz.why: The barbell plays safe where losses would be catastrophic and makes small bets to catch positive surprises.

quiz.q: After testing a hypothesis with customers in the field, what is the next step in validating the business model?
options: Consider the impact of the results on all components of the model
quiz.why: The six steps: hypothesize, design experiments, test, consider impact on all components, change the model, retest.

quiz.q: Which is one of Kim and Mauborgne's four blue ocean actions?
options: Create something the industry has never done
quiz.why: The four actions are eliminate, reduce, raise and create.

quiz.q: A platform offers basic features free and charges a subscription for enhanced features. This is…
quiz.why: Freemium mixes free basic use with paid upgrades; sponsorship has an outside entity fund free access.

quiz.q: Startups facing dominant players often focus on…
options: acquiring intellectual property and know-how attractive to a dominant firm
quiz.why: With little negotiating power, startups build controllable assets a dominant firm will want.

quiz.q: In the FreshMart analysis, what is the break-even basket for delivery?
quiz.why: Rp 12,000 delivery cost ÷ 25% gross margin = Rp 48,000. Rp 75,000 is the member minimum order, set above break-even.

quiz.q: Why does the analysis choose young working adults as FreshMart's target?
options: They are the largest group near campuses
They have steadier income and pay to save time rather than hunting discounts
quiz.why: Students buy small baskets and switch for deals; working adults score 21 of 25 and match the ready-meal line.

quiz.q: What is the biggest risk named for FreshMart Plus?
options: Members move store trips into free delivery, halving profit on those baskets
Delivery partners raise their fees to zero
quiz.why: A Rp 100,000 basket earns Rp 25,000 walked in but Rp 13,000 delivered free, so cannibalization is the key risk.

quiz.q: According to the slides, design determines as much as what share of a product's final cost?
quiz.why: Design decides features, reliability, price and appeal, and up to 80 percent of final cost.

quiz.q: What is the principal reason for new product failure, according to research cited in the slides?
options: Lack of good market and industry analysis
quiz.why: Failure rates run 70–90 percent, mainly because of weak market and industry analysis.

quiz.q: Which is one of the five problems caused by a lack of new product development resources?
quiz.why: Resource shortfalls cause poor execution, longer time to market, missed first-to-market chances, simpler projects and declining morale.

quiz.q: Prototype development belongs to which category of the product development cycle?
quiz.why: Validation and design covers feasibility, intellectual property and regulation, prototype development and market tests.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four ways to commercialize a technology listed in the slides?
options: Start a business to make and distribute it
quiz.why: The four: license, start a business, sell the technology, or joint venture.

quiz.q: For a service business, the prototype is usually…
options: a finished product sold at full price
a design, storyboard or flowchart of how the service is delivered
quiz.why: Non-manufacturing businesses still prototype, but not always physically.

quiz.q: For a product near the incremental end of the innovation spectrum, the slides suggest…
options: building a very minimal MVP in stages
building more than a simple MVP, perhaps a complete product, because customers have alternatives
waiting for competitors to launch first
quiz.why: Incremental products face strong rivals and customers who quickly judge solutions; staged MVPs suit disruptive products.

quiz.q: Outsourcing product development can cut risk, cost and cycle time by up to…
quiz.why: The slides cite reductions by factors of 60 to 90 percent.

quiz.q: Which outsourcing rule appears in the slides?
options: Never choose an outsourced partner based solely on price
Always give design and development to the same firm
Keep research and development far from customers
quiz.why: The slides warn that the lowest prices often carry the highest risk, and advise splitting design and development unless one firm specializes in both.

quiz.q: Documented, explicit knowledge that is easy to share is called…
quiz.why: Intellectual capital is tacit; intellectual assets are explicit; intellectual property carries legal rights.

quiz.q: Which form of intellectual property sits at the base of the pyramid, with the least protection?
quiz.why: The pyramid rises from trade secrets through copyrights and trademarks to patents.

quiz.q: How are trade secrets protected, according to the slides?
options: By registering them with the patent office
Only through confidentiality agreements or contracts
quiz.why: No patent or trademark law covers trade secrets; contracts are the only route.

quiz.q: Why can "aspirin" no longer be trademarked?
options: It has become part of the generic language
It was never used in commerce
Its renewal fees were too high
It uses an official state symbol
quiz.why: A trademark lasts while used and renewed, unless it becomes generic.

quiz.q: Which step in registering a trademark matters most for an international venture?
options: Testing the mark's translation in the languages of target countries
quiz.why: Descriptive marks are weak, ® is only for registered marks and marks cannot be stockpiled.

quiz.q: Under the Berne Convention, member countries must protect authors' works for at least…
options: the life of the author plus 50 years
the life of the author plus 10 years
quiz.why: The Berne minimum is life plus 50; the United States term taught is life plus 70.

quiz.q: What does a copyright protect?
options: The tangible form in which an idea is expressed
quiz.why: Copyright protects the form, not the idea; inventions are patents and brands are trademarks.

quiz.q: Which is one of the four USPTO criteria for patentability?
options: The invention must not be obvious to someone with ordinary skill in the field
The invention must already be on sale
The invention must be registered as a trademark
The invention must be at least 20 years old
quiz.why: The four: statutory class, utility, novelty (no prior art) and nonobviousness. USPTO is the United States Patent and Trademark Office.

quiz.q: A provisional patent application lasts…
quiz.why: The provisional allows "patent pending" for 12 months; the nonprovisional must follow.

quiz.q: Since the America Invents Act, which date decides between two inventors of the same invention?
options: The date of the first sale
The filing date of the patent application
quiz.why: The United States moved from first-to-invent to first-inventor-to-file.

quiz.q: A firm builds a patent portfolio to use as bargaining chips in cross-licensing. Which strategy is this?
quiz.why: Proprietary acquires patents to defend market position; defensive designs around or cross-licenses; leveraging applies when protection is not critical.

quiz.q: Under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, how long after the first filing does an applicant have to enter the national phase?
