quiz.why: File the international application within 12 months; choose national-phase countries within 30 months.

quiz.q: Within which borders does a United States patent give protection?
options: In all Patent Cooperation Treaty countries automatically
In all World Trade Organization countries
quiz.why: Patent rights stop at the border; foreign protection needs foreign filing, for example via the Patent Cooperation Treaty.

quiz.q: A case asks whether a venture should expand abroad. According to the synthesis chapter, how should the answer open?
options: With a list of every framework from the course
With a direct decision in the first lines, then the framework chain
quiz.why: Examiners reward a decision with reasons over a survey of frameworks without a verdict.

quiz.q: Which sequencing lesson is common to all three cases?
options: Expand to many markets at once
quiz.why: EuroDisney (cash before growth), FreshMart (2 stores before 25) and LocalBite (30–50 customers first) all test before scaling.

mock_exam.instructions: Answer all six questions. Marks are shown for each question and total 100. Use the course's frameworks by name, support claims with figures from the cases, and draw a diagram where it helps your answer. This paper follows the case-based style of the course; the real exam's format was not given in the course materials.

questions.q: Define entrepreneurship using Stevenson's definition and explain why the course describes the entrepreneurial process as a dynamic system rather than a linear sequence. Refer to the three phases and to the environment a new venture operates in.
questions.model_answer:
Howard Stevenson defines entrepreneurship as "the process by which individuals, either on their own or inside organizations, pursue opportunities without regard to the resources they currently control." Three parts of the definition matter. It is a process that unfolds over time, not a single decision. It can happen inside existing organizations as well as in startups. And it starts from the opportunity: entrepreneurs do not limit themselves to the money, people and equipment they already have, but gather resources once the opportunity is clear. The course adds that entrepreneurship is also a mindset, opportunity-focused, risk-taking, innovative and growth-oriented, and a set of behaviors that follow from it.

The entrepreneurial process runs in three phases. In Phase 1 the entrepreneur finds a significant problem or need, researches the industry, the market and any intellectual property, regulatory or product development issues, and turns what was learned into hypotheses. In Phase 2 those hypotheses about the customer, the solution and the business model are tested, which reveals the likely revenue sources and the major cost drivers. Only when Phases 1 and 2 give sufficient confidence that the business is feasible does Phase 3 begin: designing the business, putting the right team and partners in place, and choosing the time to launch.

The process is dynamic rather than linear for two reasons. First, the phases loop back on each other. Most hypotheses are proven wrong when tested with real customers, so a failed test in Phase 2 sends the entrepreneur back to reframe the problem or the customer in Phase 1, and the cycle may repeat several times. Second, testing does not end at launch. The new venture lives in an environment it cannot control: the economic environment, competition, new laws and regulations, labor supply and sources of capital. When any of these shifts, the business must test and adapt again. A diagram of three boxes linked by forward arrows, with a return arrow from Phase 2 to Phase 1 and the whole set inside a box labeled with the five environmental variables, captures this. EuroDisneyland illustrates the cost of treating the process as linear: a model validated in Anaheim and Tokyo was carried to France without retesting its price and cultural assumptions, and the venture lost money from its first year.

questions.q: Apply Porter's five forces to FreshMart's industry (neighborhood grocery retail with app pickup and delivery). Rate each force and conclude whether the industry is attractive for a new entrant, and how such an entrant should compete.
questions.model_answer:
Porter argues that five forces set an industry's long-run profit potential, so a venture's strategy must be based on how the industry works. Applied to neighborhood grocery retail with app ordering, the picture is as follows.

Threat of new entrants: medium. Opening a single store or a delivery-only service needs modest capital, but scale economies in purchasing, brand loyalty built through membership points, and access to good locations near homes and campuses are real barriers. FreshMart's own analysis notes that its proximity and own brand are easy to copy, which suggests barriers are not high. Threat of substitutes: high. Customers can meet the same need through traditional markets, supermarkets, minimarket chains and quick-commerce apps that deliver in minutes, or by cooking less and ordering ready meals elsewhere. Buyer power: high. Individual customers buy small amounts, but switching costs are close to zero and the case states that customers switch for discounts, so buyers can force price promotions. Supplier power: low to medium. Fresh food and household goods are available from many suppliers, and FreshMart reduces dependence further with own-brand products, although large branded suppliers retain some power. Rivalry among existing firms: high. Minimarket chains and quick-commerce firms compete on price, promotions and speed; the analysis cites Paris dark stores that needed about 1,500 orders a day to break even but averaged 150 to 250, a sign of intense, loss-making competition.

On the course's profile, an attractive industry has high entry barriers, weak buyers and suppliers, few substitutes and mild rivalry. Grocery retail shows the opposite on three of the four, so it is unattractive for a newcomer that tries to compete head-on on price. The course's advice for such markets is to avoid price wars and costly advertising battles and instead find a niche that serves an unmet need and enter quietly to gain a foothold. For a grocery entrant, that niche could be time-pressed young working adults who value fast, reliable ready meals more than discounts, the same segment the FreshMart analysis selects, served with differentiated products such as own-brand ready meals that are harder for rivals to copy than prices.

questions.q: Using the exhibits in the EuroDisneyland case, explain why the park lost money in its first year even though attendance of about 10 million exceeded the stated break-even of 7 to 8 million visitors. Support at least three causes with calculations or figures.
questions.model_answer:
EuroDisneyland opened near Paris in April 1992 and reported a net loss of FFr188 million for fiscal 1992, with cumulative losses of about $500 million by April 1993. The apparent paradox, attendance above break-even yet a loss, dissolves once the exhibits are read together. Four causes stand out.

First, the break-even target was out of date. Exhibit 5 shows construction cost estimates rising from $1.0 billion in 1985 to $4.4 billion in 1991 and $4.4 to 4.5 billion in 1992, an increase of about 4.4 times. The 7 to 8 million visitor break-even belonged to the original $1 billion plan and was never recalculated. Contributing factors in the case include construction costs about 20% above comparable United States jobs, six coats of paint on facades against one in the United States parks, $8 to 10 million of extras on Le Visionarium, and delays and modifications. In effect the project became unprofitable during construction.

Second, visitors spent too little once inside. Exhibit 6 shows EuroDisney charged the highest adult ticket of the four parks ($47) but collected the lowest total spend per person ($30 to 45). Using midpoints, the spend-to-admission ratio was $37.50 ÷ $47 ≈ 0.80×, against Tokyo's $77.50 ÷ $38 ≈ 2.04×, Anaheim's 1.81× and Orlando's 1.50×. A gap of about $40 per person against Tokyo across 10 million visitors is roughly $400 million a year, close to the cumulative loss. The likely mechanism is that an expensive ticket used up the visitor's budget before food and merchandise.

Third, the price did not fit European budgets and holiday habits. Exhibit 10 shows French income per head of $23,026 with 4.6% available for leisure, a budget of about $1,059 a year. A day at the park plus a hotel night of about $177 takes roughly 16.7% of that budget. French workers also take about five weeks of holiday, typically in long blocks spent traveling away from home, while Japanese and United States visitors take two to three weeks and favor short trips. Tokyo also had 30 million people within 30 miles and the omiage gift-giving custom; EuroDisney's market of 300 million was a day's travel away, so transport costs ate into in-park spending. The hotels' 37% occupancy shows the result.

Fourth, the deal paid Disney before profit was measured. Exhibit 8 shows Disney received 10% of admissions, 5% of food, merchandise and hotel revenue, and base management fees of 3% of revenues for five years, all charged on revenue, plus 49% of net income. Disney earned even as other shareholders lost, and cash left the business when it was most needed.

Cultural misfit reinforced all four: no alcohol in a wine-drinking country, mainly American food, a United States appearance code challenged under French labor law, and a winter climate (Paris averages 32–42°F in January against Orlando's 49–70°F) that shortened the season. Tokyo had wanted an American copy; France called the park a "cultural Chernobyl." A diagram with four cause boxes (costs, low spend, price misfit, fees on revenue) all pointing to one loss box summarizes the diagnosis.

questions.q: As Philippe Bourguignon, recommend a turnaround plan for EuroDisneyland. Compare at least three options, choose one, and justify the order in which its actions should be taken.
questions.model_answer:
Five options are available. Option A is to do nothing and wait, following Michael Eisner's view that the park will grow into the culture over time. It costs nothing now, but with cash of about FFr1.1 billion in May 1993, heavy debt and Phase Two estimated at FFr8 to 10 billion, waiting risks running out of money before the culture changes. Option B fixes the financial model: new capital, rescheduled debt and a pause on Phase Two. It buys time but leaves the product misfit untouched, so losses would return. Option C fixes the product: lower prices, wine and beer, cheaper menus and an offer adapted to European habits. It addresses the root of the low spend-to-admission ratio, but without new cash the park may not survive long enough to see the benefit. Option D sells or licenses the park, copying the Tokyo arrangement in which Disney took no equity and earned fees. It limits Disney's exposure but abandons a $160 million investment and the long-term upside, and a buyer would demand a deep discount. Option E combines B, then C, then reinvestment.

Option E is recommended because it treats both the cash crisis and its cause. The order matters, consistent with retrenchment-then-recovery turnaround thinking used in the class analysis: a firm must stop the bleeding before it can grow, and reversing the order is a common reason turnarounds fail. It also follows the course's message from feasibility analysis that a business model must be retested and changed when it meets the market.

Step 1, stabilize cash. Ask Disney to waive royalties and management fees for a period, since these are charged on revenue and drain cash regardless of profit. Use the fact that Disney risked only $160 million while lenders and French authorities had far more at stake as leverage to reschedule debt and raise new capital. Freeze Phase Two without cancelling it, to preserve it as a future attraction. Step 2, fix the offer. Cut adult ticket and hotel prices and introduce winter pricing to fit a 4.6% leisure budget and the Paris climate; serve wine and beer and add cheaper menus to remove cultural friction and raise spend per visitor; adapt employment practices so the appearance code complies with French law. Rename and market the park around its real asset, Paris, 20 miles away with 300 million people within a day's travel. Step 3, reinvest. Once cash flow is stable and spend per visitor is rising, build a major new attraction, for example from the frozen Phase Two plans, to give visitors a reason to return.

Success should be measured with the case's own indicators: spend-to-admission ratio moving from 0.80× toward the 1.5× to 2× range of other parks, hotel occupancy rising from 37%, French share of visitors rising from 29%, and a break-even recalculated on the actual $4.4 billion cost. The lesson for an international new venture is that a proven model is only a hypothesis in a new country, and price, product and financial structure must be tested against the local customer before scaling.

sections.title: Section C · Validation and protection abroad (30 marks)

questions.q: After a successful home launch, LocalBite plans to sell its frozen chili-level snack in Malaysia and Singapore. Design a validation plan before full expansion. Use feasibility analysis, the innovation spectrum and the MVP concept, and state the riskiest assumption as a testable hypothesis.
questions.model_answer:
Feasibility analysis tests, evaluates and validates a proposed business model to reduce risk before committing resources, and the course's rule is that a model proven at home is only a hypothesis abroad. LocalBite should therefore treat each block of its business model in the new markets as a hypothesis to test.

The first task is to restate the model for the new markets. The value proposition (traditional Indonesian flavor, modern presentation, customer-chosen chili level) may travel, but segments, channels, prices and costs will change. Young professionals were the primary segment at home; in Kuala Lumpur and Singapore the first customer might instead be Indonesian students and workers living abroad, a niche with a strong existing need. Channels change too: frozen food needs cold-chain delivery and local platforms, and import and food registration rules apply in each country. The three critical success questions must be answered for each market: is the segment large enough to be viable and grow, do the capital needs to reach positive cash flow make sense, and can a team or partner be assembled locally?

On the innovation spectrum the product is incremental: frozen snacks are known and rivals exist, so customers can compare and have alternatives. The course advises that near the incremental end a very simple MVP will not produce useful feedback; the test product should be close to complete, with real packaging, price and delivery. The MVP should therefore be a small, real offer rather than a mock-up: a limited batch sold through one channel in one city.

The riskiest assumption is demand at a price that covers the higher cost of export and cold-chain delivery. As a testable hypothesis: "We believe Indonesian students and young professionals in Kuala Lumpur will buy at least two packs a month at a price that gives at least our home gross margin after shipping and platform fees." The experiment runs in two stages, mirroring FreshMart's approach. In weeks 1 to 2, a fake-door test: an order page and pre-order (PO) list promoted through Indonesian student associations, counting sign-ups before shipping anything. In weeks 3 to 10, a pilot: one shipment sold through direct orders and one local delivery platform, with Singapore held back as the comparison market. The measures are conversion from sign-up to purchase, repeat purchase in month two, and contribution per pack after shipping and commission. The pass condition is positive contribution per pack and a majority of buyers reordering. Following the six-step validation loop, the results are then traced across the whole model (for example, a weak margin may require a higher price or a local co-packer), the model is changed, and the test is rerun before entering Singapore. This keeps most of the business safe, in line with Taleb's barbell, while a small bet tests the upside.

questions.q: Advise LocalBite on protecting its brand, recipe and packaging design as it expands to Malaysia and Singapore. Identify the appropriate form of intellectual property for each asset, explain the timing issues, and say whether a patent is worthwhile.
questions.model_answer:
The course ranks intellectual property (IP) by degree of protection in a pyramid: trade secrets at the base, then copyrights, trademarks and patents. Each LocalBite asset fits a different level, and each has its own timing rule.

The recipe and process, including the method of mixing chili into the dough and the portioning that creates eleven chili levels from one batch, are best protected as trade secrets. Under the Uniform Trade Secrets Act definition taught in the course, a trade secret is a formula, process or compilation of information that gives a competitive advantage, is not common knowledge and is kept reasonably confidential. There is no registration; protection comes only from confidentiality agreements or contracts. LocalBite should therefore have any co-packer, distributor or employee in Malaysia or Singapore sign confidentiality agreements before seeing the recipe, and limit who knows the full process. If a signatory misappropriates it, remedies include injunctive relief, damages and attorney's fees. Week 6's caution applies: outsourcing production to places where enforcement is weak makes secrets harder to protect.

The brand name and logo should be protected as trademarks. A trademark identifies a business or product in commerce and lasts as long as it is used and renewed. Registration gives enhanced rights, and because the first to file generally holds the presumptive right to a mark, LocalBite should file in Malaysia and Singapore before launching there; its home registration helps applications abroad. Before filing, it should search existing marks, check that the name is distinctive rather than merely descriptive, test the name's translation and connotations in Malay, Chinese and Tamil, and choose the product categories to protect, such as frozen snacks. After registration it can record the mark with customs authorities to block counterfeit imports.

The packaging artwork, photographs and social media content are protected by copyright, which covers the tangible form of original work rather than the idea. Protection exists once the work is fixed, and the Berne Convention means member countries protect works from other members for at least the life of the author plus 50 years. LocalBite should still mark its packaging with ©, the year and the owner's name, keep records of creation, and use cease and desist letters against copiers.

A patent is unlikely to be worthwhile. The course's signals for patenting are an invention that solves a significant problem and changes how things are done, falls under food and drug regulation, earns more than enforcement would cost, or will be licensed. A snack recipe change is probably not novel or nonobvious enough to meet the patentability criteria, the product's economic life in a fast-moving snack market may be short, and filing would publish the method, destroying its value as a trade secret. If LocalBite did develop a genuinely new process, the timing rule is strict: under first-to-file, it should file promptly, and to cover Malaysia and Singapore it would file a Patent Cooperation Treaty application within 12 months of its first filing and enter the national phase in chosen countries by month 30. In strategy terms, LocalBite fits a leveraging approach to patents, where proprietary patent protection is not critical, while relying on trade secrets for the recipe and trademarks for the brand.
